question: What is the Definition of Done, and what happens to a Product Backlog item that doesn't meet it?
text:
The Definition of Done (DoD) is a formal description of the state of the product Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product[1]. It serves as the official commitment for the Scrum Increment artifact, creating transparency by giving the Scrum Team and stakeholders a shared understanding of what work was completed[1][2]. It encapsulates agreed-upon team criteria regarding quality, testing, assurance, and non-functional requirements that every item must satisfy[3][4]. The exact moment a Product Backlog item satisfies the Definition of Done, an Increment is born[1].
If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, the following rules apply:
It cannot be released: Work cannot be considered part of an Increment unless it meets the Definition of Done, meaning it cannot be delivered to users[1][5].
It cannot be presented at the Sprint Review: Incomplete items must not be shown or demonstrated during the Sprint Review, as presenting unfinished work can erode trust with stakeholders[1][6].
It returns to the Product Backlog: The item is sent back to the Product Backlog for future consideration and re-prioritization by the Product Owner and team[1].
No partial credit is awarded: The team does not receive partial story points or incomplete work credit for the Sprint[7].
💡 Would you like to explore how the Definition of Done differs from the Definition of Ready, or see guidance on how teams collaboratively create one?

Developers
Developers are the people in the Scrum Team that are committed to creating any aspect of a usable
Increment each Sprint.
The specific skills needed by the Developers are often broad and will vary with the domain of work.
However, the Developers are always accountable for:
• Creating a plan for the Sprint, the Sprint Backlog;
• Instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done;
• Adapting their plan each day toward the Sprint Goal; and,
• Holding each other accountable as professionals.

Tips  
• This is not a status meeting. Rather, it is an opportunity for stakeholders to collaborate with the team and improve the Product Backlog with shared context and learnings.
• Don’t demonstrate work that isn’t “ Done .” It can significantly erode trust between the Scrum Team , stakeholders, and end users if the demonstrated work doesn’t get shipped as expected. It also allows the Scrum Team to persist the illusion that incomplete work is still valuable. Remember: work in process is a liability, not an asset. ( ap.tips/toc )
